spec.summary: M3: GET /health reports real database and upstream state. M8: every database operation is time-bounded (5 s query, 5 s connection acquire, 30 s overall startup) and a timeout in a request path is a 503, never a 500. Constants only, no new settings. No git state changes; CLAUDE.md is updated by the orchestrator (text at the end).
spec.user_stories: - As an operator or load balancer, I can call /health and learn whether Postgres and the Finnhub upstream are actually working, not just that the process is alive. - As an API client, a stuck or locked database makes my rules/alerts request fail fast with 503 instead of hanging. - As an operator, a Postgres that accepts connections but never finishes startup work makes the app exit with a clear "startup failed: ... timed out" line instead of hanging forever. - As a user, price ingestion keeps flowing while the database is slow or stuck.

constants.where: backend/app/db.py, module level, one-line comment each, no Settings/.env entries

design.constants: DB_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 5.0 (per-query limit, passed as command_timeout to asyncpg.create_pool) DB_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 5.0 (max wait to get a pooled connection; passed as timeout= to every pool.acquire) DB_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 30.0 (one overall limit for connect + DDL + backfill + load rules + load watchlist) HEALTH_DB_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 2.0 (limit for the /health SELECT 1 probe, covers acquire and query) The HEALTH constant is the "about 2 s" from the request; it is a fourth named constant, still no setting.
design.acquire_call_sites: Every pool.acquire() in db.py gets timeout=DB_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (12 existing sites): connect (schema DDL), _tick_worker, save_rule, delete_rule, list_rules, load_rules, create_rule_with_watchlist, load_watchlist, _backfill_watchlist, _write_alert_rows (batch attempt AND the row-by-row retry), list_alerts. The new probe (below) is the 13th site and uses HEALTH_DB_TIMEOUT_SECONDS instead. Constants are read at call time (module-global lookup) so tests can monkeypatch app.db.<NAME>. asyncpg.create_pool gets command_timeout=DB_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_SECONDS in addition to the existing min/max/timeout arguments (the existing create_pool connect timeout=5 and outer wait_for 10 are left as they are).
design.timeout_exceptions: asyncpg raises asyncio.TimeoutError for a command_timeout expiry, and asyncio.TimeoutError for an acquire timeout (on Python 3.11+ this is the builtin TimeoutError). Both derive from Exception, so the existing `except Exception` blocks in routers/rules.py (_unavailable) and routers/alerts.py already map them to 503 "rule storage unavailable" / "alert storage unavailable". No router code change is required; the requirement is that this stays true and is covered by tests. CancelledError is not an Exception and must not be swallowed. Routers log only the exception type (existing behaviour); a timeout logs "TimeoutError". Writers: _tick_worker and _write_alert_rows already catch Exception, so a timeout is a failed write (tick: logged and dropped; alert: failed batch, row retry, ALERT_FAILURE_BACKOFF_SECONDS sleep). No change needed beyond the new timeouts; Services.on_tick stays non-blocking.
design.startup: Services._load_state wraps its whole body (db.connect(), the persistence-disabled early return, the available check, rule_store.load(), db.load_watchlist()) in one asyncio.wait_for with DB_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, read through the db module at call time (e.g. `from . import db as db_module`) so tests can patch app.db.DB_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS. On asyncio.TimeoutError, log at ERROR exactly one line beginning "startup failed:" and containing "timed out" and "RULES_PERSISTENCE_ENABLED=false", e.g. "startup failed: Postgres setup timed out after 30s; set RULES_PERSISTENCE_ENABLED=false to run without it" (seconds printed from the constant), then re-raise (any exception type, e.g. RuntimeError). The line contains no exception text, URL, or credential. The existing Services.startup except-branch (db.close(), upstream never started) is reused unchanged, so the pool and workers are released. The existing handler for load errors (which interpolates the exception text) must not be the one that handles timeouts: handle TimeoutError first. A TimeoutError raised from inside a query (command_timeout) during load_rules/load_watchlist is also reported with the same "timed out" line. The opt-out path (persistence false) is subject to the same wrapper but returns immediately.
design.health: Response model: exactly three body keys {"status","database","upstream"}; no other fields, no messages, no URLs. Router: routers/health.py reads request.app.state.services (same access pattern as the other routers); /health stays on `app` outside the /api key-protected router (tests/test_api_auth_coverage.py still passes). database: "disabled" = settings.rules_persistence_enabled is False (explicit opt-out). Not a failure; no probe is made. "ok" = flag true and a probe succeeded: a new Database.ping() (async, returns bool) acquires a connection (HEALTH_DB_TIMEOUT_SECONDS) and runs SELECT 1 bounded by the same limit. "down" = flag true and the probe fails, times out, or raises anything (Exception), OR flag true and there is no pool (db.available is False). The no-pool case cannot occur after a successful fail-loud start; it is defined as "down" because persistence is required but unusable. ping() never raises (except CancelledError), returns False when _pool is None, and logs at most the exception type name (no message). upstream: "disabled" = services.upstream is None (no Finnhub key). "connected" = upstream.connected is True. "disconnected" = upstream exists and connected is not True. status: "ok" when database in (ok, disabled) and upstream in (connected, disabled); otherwise "degraded". HTTP: 503 when database == "down" (body still the same three fields, status "degraded"); otherwise 200 (including upstream disconnected, status "degraded"). Health uses db.ping(), not db.available, because available only means "a pool object exists".
design.test_doubles: FakeDatabase (tests/fakes/fake_db.py): add `async def ping(self) -> bool` returning `not self.failing` and, optionally, raising/awaiting forever per a settable attribute (e.g. ping_error / ping_hang) so the router-level time bound can be tested. FakeFinnhubClient (tests/fakes/fake_finnhub.py): add a public `connected` attribute (default False) so health tests can set True.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: Lock test: with a second asyncpg connection holding `LOCK TABLE alert_rules IN ACCESS EXCLUSIVE MODE` in an open transaction, GET /api/rules, POST /api/rules, and DELETE /api/rules/{id} (and GET /api/alerts with the lock on `alerts`) each return 503 within a small multiple of the patched limit (assert elapsed under ~3 s) instead of hanging. After the lock transaction is rolled back, the same requests succeed (pool still healthy, no leaked connections: a subsequent request works). The test must roll back and close the holder connection in a finally block so the cleanup that drops tables does not deadlock.

/health against a real, healthy Postgres returns database "ok"; with the pool closed or the database stopped it reports "down" with 503 (stopping is not required; closing the pool via db._close_pool() suffices).

spec.ambiguities_resolved: 1. "disabled" vs "down": disabled only for the explicit opt-out flag; flag true with no pool or a failed probe is "down". 2. Overall status when database is "down": "degraded" (with 503). 3. Fourth constant for the health probe (HEALTH_DB_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 2.0) is added although the request lists three numbers; no setting. 4. Probe lives in a new Database.ping() because health must not touch pool internals and FakeDatabase needs a matching method. 5. Startup 30 s wraps the whole _load_state (including the persistence-disabled branch), is read at call time via the db module so tests can patch it; timeouts are handled before the generic load-error handler to keep exception text out of the log. 6. connect() swallows its own errors into last_error; a startup timeout cancels it mid-flight, so the existing startup except-branch (db.close()) is what releases the pool. 7. Routers need no code change: asyncio.TimeoutError is an Exception and already maps to 503; tests prove it. 8. FakeFinnhubClient gets connected=False by default, so default fake-upstream health is "degraded". 9. The alert writer's row-by-row retry after a batch timeout is left as is (each row can wait up to 5 s acquire + 5 s query); changing retry policy is out of scope.
spec.assumptions: - Python 3.11+ semantics apply, or asyncio.TimeoutError is caught explicitly so it works on older versions too. - asyncpg's command_timeout applies to executemany and transactional statements, including pg_advisory_xact_lock. - A statement timeout mid-transaction leaves the pooled connection reset by asyncpg on release (no manual cleanup). - /health does not require the lifespan to have run beyond what TestClient-as-context-manager provides.
spec.edge_cases: - Probe hangs: /health still answers within about HEALTH_DB_TIMEOUT_SECONDS. - Concurrent /health calls while the pool is saturated: acquire times out, reports "down" (503), not a hang. - upstream object without a `connected` attribute: treated as not connected, never an AttributeError/500. - Startup timeout after the pool was created: pool closed, workers cancelled, upstream never started. - create_rule_with_watchlist times out while holding the advisory lock inside a transaction: 503, the rule is not in rule_store, the watchlist is not changed in memory. - Timeout during delete: 503, rule remains in rule_store. - /health response must never include exception text, connection URL, or key.

risks.risk: The hanging-request tests can hang the suite if a timeout is not applied; every such test must wrap the request in an outer bound (e.g. a thread/anyio timeout) so a regression fails instead of freezing.
Real-Postgres lock test: the holder connection must be released or the per-test table DROP in the fixture will block on the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock.
A 5 s command_timeout also bounds the startup DDL/backfill on a large table; the 30 s overall limit is the backstop. Acceptable per the user decision.
An orchestrator probe such as docker healthcheck hitting /health will now see 503 when the DB is down; that is the intent.
Row-by-row alert retry after a timeout can keep the writer busy for a long time (see ambiguity 9); ingestion is unaffected because enqueue is non-blocking.

(2) Invariant 5 addition: "Every database operation is time-bounded by constants in db.py: DB_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (5), DB_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (5), DB_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (30, startup fails loudly with 'startup failed: ... timed out'), HEALTH_DB_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (2); a timeout in a request path is a 503, in a writer a failed write." (3) Remove any statement that /health is a plain liveness check, and note tests' acquire() doubles must accept timeout=.
spec.self_critique: Every story maps to a criterion (health 1-7, request timeouts 8-10 and 13, startup 11, ingestion 12). Each criterion names its test. Biggest remaining uncertainty: whether asyncpg actually surfaces command_timeout as a plain asyncio.TimeoutError for pg_advisory_xact_lock inside a transaction on the pinned version, and the cancelled connect() leaving a half-built pool; criterion 13 and 11 are the real-world checks that settle both.
